translation.en: the winds, or their blessing (what Skyborne greetings and farewells invoke)
translation.uk: вітри або їхнє благословення (те, що закликають привітання і прощання небесонароджених)

notes: Darnassian (Skyborne dialect). In all four elvish formulas of the Skyborne voice files: banu alah and banu adora (greetings), aradash ... banu (a greeting) and aeesha'el banu zephrali (a farewell), and written once in the letter MailTemplate 652. It takes the place of Elune in Darnassian Elune-adore 'Elune be with you' and of ishnu 'good fortune' in Ishnu-alah 'good fortune to you', so it names what the blessing wishes on the listener. Almost every English blessing of the same NPC voices invokes the winds ('Gale's greetings, friend', 'Blessing of the winds upon you', 'May the winds guide your path'; only 'May you always land with grace' and 'The Skysight will guide you' do not), as does the player /welcome 'Winds welcome you', and the letter that ends with banu says 'I am unsure where the winds will lead you'. In all, 25 of the 49 English greetings and farewells of those voices mention the wind; most of the rest are shop lines and plain hellos and goodbyes. Whether banu is the winds themselves or their blessing is open. Replaces the low 'way, passage' guess of report 3. A person listening to all 12 elvish lines (2026-11-18) hears the stress on the second syllable every time: ba-NU.

notes: Darnassian (Skyborne dialect). The female player voice says it for /hello, beside the English hellos 'Hello', 'Land with grace' and 'Gale's greetings, friend'; two Skyborne NPC voice sets say it as a greeting. The male /hello was heard as 'anu ala' by three of four listeners and 'Benu Allah' by one: probably the same phrase with a weak b. Built like Darnassian Ishnu-alah 'good fortune to you', with alah 'to you' (the Thalassian homograph alah 'light' fits a greeting less well); compare the English greeting of the same NPC voice, probably 'Favorable winds to you, friend' (heard only by Wizper, as 'wins'). Spelled alah after Ishnu-alah; the listeners heard Allah, ala or alah. A person listening (2026-11-18) hears ba-NU, and the final h of alah usually but faintly, which supports the spelling alah.
